On the other hand, the majority of deaths occurred on days of only moderate heat.  One thing that was both shocking but predictable is that of the deaths that occurred inside, all residences had air conditioners but were listed as not functioning.  I'm unclear if that includes AC's that just weren't on because of high energy costs which is something we all have likely heard about. If you're planning to - or fortunate enough to - live a long life in the U.S., you'd better be very well off financially. Old age is not kind to fragile, illness and/or dementia stricken, penniless elders in this country. 

Who is going to take care of you when you can no longer drive, walk, get yourself to the bathroom, shop, prepare your meals, and so forth? Excellent, clean private care facilities (Independent Living, Assisted Living, Memory Care) cost up to $10,000 a month and sometimes much more. The alternative is a state-run nursing home and often conditions are deplorable. Not everyone who has family who can take in fragile elders, and even when family can do that, the toll on the caregiver (usually the daughter) is tremendous.

I don't mean to sound cynical, but I work with elders and I've seen what happens when one grows old without funds or assets. I've seen the toll of having zero options for getting supportive care. 

And every time I read comments from elders who are so very happy past the age of 75 or 80 or beyond, I automatically assume that they are among the wealthy, with enough money for secure housing, hired transportation, excellent medical and dental care, and extras like house cleaners, gardeners, and a way to secure meals without having to shop or cook very much at all.

I've said it before and I'll say it again: if you're going to be old in America, you'd better be rich. It's the only buffer against suffering.

I spent last weekend in Norway, visiting relatives. They asked me what I'm now doing in my "retirement." I explained to them that I'm not actually retired in the way that they understand it, because I now spend 30-40 hours/week doing volunteer work providing social services to our poor, our elderly, immigrant communities, etc. I told them that until I retired 3 years ago, I had no idea that so much of the important social services are provided by volunteers and retirees like me.

They were shocked to hear that most Americans expect critical services to be provided by volunteers instead of our government.

We also went to Poland, for a few days. In neither country did we see poverty like we see in both urban and rural areas throughout the US. Infrastructure like roads and public transportation are efficient and well-kept. Most middle-class Europeans enjoy 3-4 weeks of vacation each summer, and many travel internationally during it. Minimum wage in Poland is $8.40, even for waiters and taxi drivers. Everyone seemed so much happier than in the US, even shopkeepers and service workers.

And most people there are more well versed in international politics than most Americans.

My Norwegian cousin asked us "What's going on in America?" A Republican relative answered "The main problem is that we're divided as a country." I retorted "No, the actual problem is that most Americans accept the lies coming from Trump and Fox News." The Norwegian smiled and nodded surreptitiously.

I would much rather pay higher taxes to provide  fair national comprehensive support to people who need it.  Better yet, as you suggest, divert funds from unpopular losing wars and genocidal regimes.

I used to work as a forester for street trees in NYC. Poo-shoe was a common rookie problem.

I actually contacted Cornell Cooperative Extension to gather information about the dung beetles and other scat-eating creatures found in the region, and the issue that keeps dog poo from breaking down for days is the medications we give pets to prevent and treat all sorts of parasites. Things like ivermectin that prevent dogs from getting sick wind up in their poop. This makes the fecal matter toxic to beetle and fly larva that would break it down.

That also means any effort to compost dog poop will be hampered as the medical byproducts in the poop dramatically slow down decomposition. Composting is great, but it isn't the solution here. Music was mixed and mastered with real intention because of the inherent restrictions of analog gear, tape hiss and the discipline of not running a signal too hot. I'm doing my best ever since I saw An Inconvenient Truth twenty years ago and knew we had to be our own saviors. But especially in these last few years as it is becoming more obvious how we humans have changed our climate and what that means for us, other species, and generations to come. 

I've insulated my house, put on solar panels, gotten an entry level EV and charger in my garage and a heat pump to heat and cool my small home.  I encourage all those who are able to go electric to do so.

What has given me the most joy is planting native shrubs, flowers, grasses and trees in my small yard for the pollinators and birds. The loss of biodiversity is a twin crisis to climate change.  Additionally, France has strict, communicated laws for individuals, businesses and towns requiring the clearing of brush around buildings and roads  (power lines a good idea too?)... laws that are simply NOT enforced or respected.  (The same lack of enforcement of clearing happened in Hawaii's 2023 tragic fire & the 2018 Paradise fire in California.)

We had a few fires begin in Switzerland too every year where 32% of the total land area is forests and mountain, so quite difficult fire risk/management terrain. The difference in damage is strict building material codes & proper fire preventing clearing that is done everywhere - farmers & loggers are even subsidised to manage the needed clearing and control of woodlands all year long to avoid fires while individuals & localities manage the rest of brush clearing near them.

Prevention is possibly to be considered first?  The choice otherwise can be very costly in property and lives.

Regurgitate comes from Latin ‘re‘ (back) and ‘gurgitare’ (to flood/swallow), from ‘gurges’ (whirlpool/abyss). Originally used for fluids flowing backward, it evolved to mean throwing up food.

Related Words

Gorge: From ‘throat’; now a deep valley or stuffing oneself with food.

Gorgeous: From neck clothing or necklaces; shifted to mean beautiful.

Gargle / Gurgle: Echoic, onomatopoeic words for throat sounds and bubbling water.

Every human compares themself to others, it’s ingrained and natural within us. Example is, “they look good in purple, I don’t”. That can turn into envy. And like the article mentioned, it is most likely a proxy for something or some quality you want for yourself. Introspection is good here, from here it can move onto working on yourself if one is introspective and thoughtful (bring that thing/quality into your own life with your own flavor and personalization). But a lot of the times it veers off into competition quickly because humans are emotional and a lot of people are not very introspective or knowledgeable about their subconscious drives. comments.body: I agree with another commenter who wrote that it's unlikely your mom will live for 10 years or more, and that her ability to travel will rapidly diminish. Instead of thinking about your mother's time left on earth in vast, unknown spans of time, what if you thought about what the next 6 months to one year might look like, for you and your family, and build a manageable plan for these short blocks? Then, readjust as needed as your mother's health continues to decline. Is it possible that the reason you're experiencing a stressful relationship with your sibling is that they're spending far more time helping your mom, and this is building resentment? This could be a good time to discuss what end of life care looks like for your mom, and acknowledge to your sibling whatever work they're doing that may be more than what you're capable of doing given the distance. The situation does sound incredibly stressful and draining, but it's not permanent - nor will whatever decisions you make satisfy everyone. Best wishes to you as you navigate this very sad time.

Nobody is obligated to do the bidding of anyone simply because they are dying. However, LW’s mother is unlikely to have much time left during which she’s well enough to travel. So, it doesn’t seem LW would be agreeing to a decade’s worth of family vacations. Family dynamics are complicated and can be very stressful. But the dying mother’s desire to gather her whole family around her for a last trip is, as the ethicist points out, deeply human and understandable. 

In LW’s shoes, I would agree to one big family trip sooner rather than later and after that would feel less likely to repeat the gesture. And I would do my best to make that trip as pleasant as possible, even if it meant biting my tongue for a week or two. In addition to giving mom pleasure in her final days, I would view it as modeling behavior for my children. One day they will be the adults and LW will be the dying parent.

This is a great educational tool, but the parameters that were set reinforce ideas that this land was unsettled, open, waiting to be “civilized”. This story is a laudable contribution to current dialogues. However, it systematically obscures and renders invisible what came before & continues to exist. Immigration to the US began before the US existed. 

The historical processes associated with “settling” native territories is a meaningful thread that sits under & beside this story.  Settlers did not come to an uninhabited continent & the history of immigration to the US  is more complex than the story presented. Political and historical context is missing in this text for every era.

Additional maps (data is readily available) that illustrate the multitudes of tribal nations and communities who lived on this continent as settlers arrived & as the United States moved westward are important elements of this story.  This is a significant failure, because the story presented fuels the notion that “Americans” were always here & this is the “American” birthright. Timelines & maps that illustrate the  contexts & processes that promoted & encouraged settlement & later fueled immigration from across the globe would be helpful.

This story provides important information, but the narrative is incomplete.

comments.name: Barbara Lekatsas
comments.body: I was one of those listeners that couldn’t stop listening to Graceland. I was a follower of Simon and Garfunkel, then Paul Simon alone and still have the LPs to prove it. The songs in Graceland are a fusion not just of the sounds of different cultures but offer in their lyrics an American odyssey filled with “miracle and wonder” in the characters they conjure with poetic double entendres such as “diamonds on the soles of her feet,” stunning similes, “the Mississippi delta was shining like a national guitar” …”And she said, "losing love/Is like a window in your heart/Everybody sees you're blown apart/Everybody sees the wind blow"…there’s a vulnerability to the songs. He does social critique but rarely vilifies his characters. The voice itself is almost quiet, but then, there is this driving music. The music of Graceland and Rhythm of the Saints is spectacular. I was a runner and a new mom when these albums came out and I played them while I ran. I was so enchanted by the percussion on You Can Call Me All” and The Obvious Child” in The Rhythm of the Saints that I decided to learn how to drum and went to Harbor Conservatory for the Performing Arts in East Harlem and studied bongos for four years with the fantastic Victor Rendon. Thank you, Paul Simon. I will read the book by Ashley Kahn. From my listener’s point of view, the Black African contribution is the key to its great sound and the album introduced me to a group of great artists that I was unaware of.

And it's not about race, class, or 'cultural appropriation' as much as people want it to be. I mean look at the recent success of Jon Baptiste with his gospel Mozart and blues Beethoven. It's about the love of great music and what sounds good and moves you. Graceland is one of the greatest creations of pop music history, and yes it owes a lot to South African music and deliberately so. comments.name: Anne Richter
comments.body: The US administration seems to have gone out of its way to punish Asian nations with severe tariffs. For many the notion of a commonality of interests has been shattered. The tariffs in combination with the closure of Hormuz has created significant economic strains as well as currency problems. Why would the majority of these states continue to assume indefinitely that the US is either a friend or a protector? Some may  begin to question whether the US has a legitimate role in Asia at all. The Philippines has an historical relationship with the US, but its long term strategic trajectory is not guaranteed. Other states have enjoyed no special relationship with the US; however, all have experienced trading, political and cultural relationships with China over many centuries. What is the US trying to achieve in Asia?

It makes it really hard not to wonder whether maybe that's the whole point of this war, for which we still have not received a convincing explanation for we entered into in the first place.

comments.body: I take issue with the cue "spine pressed into the floor." Physical therapists just want you to engage your abdominals enough so that you're not arching away from the floor. For many clients, pressing the spine into the floor could result in a compressed abdominal wall and shoulders that are not activating away from the ears. Just activate the abdominals enough to protect the lower back and the coordination of the breathing with the maneuver should do the rest.
